passages.text:
When Simon heard this, he said, “You will not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose. For it is possible both to think and to speak about his essence—I mean by starting from the good qualities belonging to human beings. For example, both living and dying belong to a human being, but to God belongs not dying, but living—and living eternally. Again, being evil or good belongs to human beings, but to God belongs being incomparably good. And, so that I may not prolong the argument at length, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings belong eternally to God.”

Peter said, “Tell me, Simon: does it belong to human beings to beget evil and good people and to do evil and good things?”

Simon said, “It does.”

Peter said, “Since you have spoken this way, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings must be assigned to God. Since human beings beget evil and good people, God can beget only good people; and since human beings do evil and good things, he himself delights in doing only good things. Thus, concerning God, either one cannot speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and must remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings. In this way, he alone is the cause of all good things.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὐ δυσωπήσεις με περὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ σιωπή[σαν]τα περὶ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ [ζη]τεῖν μόνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: You will not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπέω can mean to put someone under pressure or make someone feel constrained. The rendering preserves σιωπήσαντα as prior to ζητεῖν; “shame me ... into investigating” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about his essence
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὐσία denotes God’s being or essence here, whereas the plural οὐσίαι in the following section denotes elemental substances.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the better of the qualities belonging to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσόντα denotes attributes or qualities that belong to someone, and κρείττονα selects those regarded as superior.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ δὲ θεῷ τὸ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀγαθῷ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to God belongs being incomparably good
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσυγκρίτῳ may describe goodness as incomparable or function adverbially as “incomparably”; the latter gives natural English without changing the claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως π[ερὶ θεοῦ] ἢ οὐ τὰ ἀνθρώποις προσόντα λέγειν καὶ σιωπᾶν ἔστιν ἢ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus, concerning God, either one cannot speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and must remain silent, or
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first member is compressed. The rendering understands οὐ with λέγειν and takes καὶ σιωπᾶν as the resulting alternative; a more formally possible reading is “either it is not possible to say these things and to remain silent.”

passages.text:
Simon said, “Therefore, if God is the cause only of good things, what remains to be understood except that some other first principle begot the evil one, or that he is perhaps unbegotten?”

Peter said, “Neither did some other power beget the evil one, nor is evil unbegotten, as I shall show at the end. For my present task is to demonstrate—as I promised at the beginning—that God is blameless in every respect. We have therefore granted that God possesses, beyond comparison, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings. Consequently, he can also be the one who puts forth the four substances—I mean hot and cold, wet and dry. Since these are primary, simple, and unmixed, they have no inclination toward either side; but after being put forth by God and blended outside him, they became a living being possessing the purpose of destroying evil people. And so, although all things have been generated from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his evil from God himself, who made everything and in whom it is impossible for evil to exist. For the substances, being neutral, were carefully distinguished and put forth from him; and when outside him they had been blended with one another by his skill, the desire for the destruction of evil people arose by an act of will. But the evil that arose cannot destroy good people, not even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. Thus the evil one, being ignorant of each person’s character, gains experience concerning them and, after thoroughly examining them, punishes them.”

Simon said, “Therefore, since God has the power to mix the elements and to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise, why did he not make each person’s mixture disposed to choose good things?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: some other first principle begot
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχή may mean a beginning, source, or ruling first principle. “First principle” fits the proposed independent origin of the evil one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be the one who puts forth the four substances
lexical_decisions.rationale: προβολεύς describes one who projects or puts something forth. The rendering preserves the emanative image without importing a later technical system.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they have no inclination toward either side
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὐδέτερον leaves the two opposed sides implicit, contextually good and evil; the translation does not insert them into the text.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γενέσθαι ζῷον, προ[αί]ρεσιν ἔχον ὀλοθρεῦσαι κακούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: they became a living being possessing the purpose of destroying evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural substances become a singular ζῷον through blending. προαίρεσις here is its purposive disposition, not necessarily an isolated act of choice.

lexical_decisions.chosen: carefully distinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rare form conveys deliberate discrimination or separation. “Carefully selected” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ πρὸς τὸν τῶν κακῶν ὄλεθρον ἐπιθυμία
lexical_decisions.chosen: the desire for the destruction of evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν κακῶν may denote evil people or evil things. The personal sense is favored by the preceding κακούς and the subsequent contrast with ἀγαθούς.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after thoroughly examining them, punishes them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διελέγχω can mean examine, expose, refute, or prove guilty. “Thoroughly examining” fits the preceding statement that the evil one initially does not know each person’s character.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποιεῖν κράσει[ς] πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make mixtures for whatever ends he wishes, so that whatever purposes he wishes may arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated relatives and shift from neuter ἃ to feminine ἃς make the attachment compressed. The rendering relates the first phrase to the intended ends and the second to προαιρέσεις; alternatively, ἃς may refer back directly to κράσεις.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disposed to choose good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαιρετικός with the genitive describes an inclination or capacity to choose the specified objects.

source_issues.issue: The printed period after the article has no intelligible syntactic function. It is treated as a typographic or editorial punctuation feature rather than as a sentence boundary.

passages.text: Peter said, “Our present task is to show how the evil one came to be—if indeed he did come to be—and by whom. As for whether he came to be blamelessly, when I have completed the argument now before us, I will then show how and why he came to be, and I will establish that the one who made him is blameless. Nevertheless, we said that the four substances were put forth by God, and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the purpose directed against evil people arose just as he wished. For if it had arisen contrary to his purpose, or from some other substance or even some other cause, God’s plan would not have been secure, since rulers of evil might continually arise against his will and wage war against his designs. But it is impossible for matters to be this way. For no living being—and especially one fit to rule—can come into being by accident, since everything that comes into being must come into being through someone.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: As for whether he came to be blamelessly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical, with ἐγένετο understood from the preceding clause. It concerns whether the evil one’s coming-to-be occurred without blame attaching to the maker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the purpose directed against evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive could formally yield “the choice of evil things.” The preceding description, however, explicitly gives the being a purpose to destroy κακούς, favoring an objective genitive directed against evil people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s plan would not have been secure
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, this is “the firmness of the plan.” The English rendering expresses the plan’s settled reliability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rulers of evil might continually arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: κακίας may characterize what these rulers govern or embody. “Leaders in wickedness” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν γὰρ ζῷον καὶ ταῦτα ἡ[γε]μονικὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: no living being—and especially one fit to rule—
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα emphasizes an additional noteworthy circumstance: the being is not merely alive but ruling or fitted to command.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by accident
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes coming about incidentally or as a mere chance occurrence, in contrast with production by an agent.

passages.text:
Simon said, “What then? Does matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him, put forth rulers against him as an enemy, rulers who hinder his designs?”

Peter said, “If matter is eternal, it is not anyone’s enemy. For what exists forever is also incapable of suffering; and being incapable of suffering, it is blessed; and being blessed, it cannot become receptive to enmity, since, in eternal creation, it has no fear of being deprived of anything. Why, rather, does matter not love the Creator, since it is seen bringing forth fruits as food for all those generated by him? And why does it not fear him as the stronger, since it also acknowledges this by trembling through earthquakes? And when it surged into great waves while the Teacher was sailing, then quickly obeyed when he commanded calm and became quiet? What then? Did the demons not come out while both fearing and honoring him? And did not others first plead for permission to enter pigs, since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ὕλη αὐτῷ σύγχρονος οὖσα καὶ ἰσοδύναμος
lexical_decisions.chosen: matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύγχρονος here means existing during the same eternal duration as God, while ἰσοδύναμος asserts equal power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: incapable of suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπαθής can mean unaffected, impassible, or incapable of suffering. The argument links it with freedom from loss and fear, so the fuller reader-facing expression is used.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀιδίῳ κτίσει στερηθῆναί τινος μὴ πεφοβημένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: since, in eternal creation, it has no fear of being deprived of anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἀιδίῳ κτίσει has uncertain attachment. The main rendering treats it as a dative of sphere; “by an eternal creation” or “as an eternal created thing” are grammatically conceivable but contextually difficult alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when it surged into great waves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression describes the sea, as matter, rising or surging in large waves.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while both fearing and honoring him
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω can mean prefer, esteem highly, or honor. The implied object is the Teacher, as in the surrounding questions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μηδὲ τοῦ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν’ ἄνευ τῆς αὐτοῦ συγχωρήσεως ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς introduces the basis implied by their request, and συγχώρησις here denotes permission or consent.

passages.text:
Simon said, “What then? Although matter is inanimate, does it have a nature capable of producing evil things and good things?”

Peter said, “According to this argument, it is neither good nor evil, because it does not act by choice, being inanimate and insensible. Consequently, here too one can discern how, although it is inanimate, it puts forth animate beings, and how, although it is insensible, it appears to create skillfully formed shapes, both those of animals and those of plants.”

Simon said, “What then? If God himself gave it life, does he not himself exist as the cause of evils while this matter gives birth?”

Peter said, “If God gave it life according to his will, his spirit operates it, and there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or beyond his power, because everything that comes into being through him comes into being as he wishes. But you will say, ‘He himself is the cause of evil, if indeed he himself produces evil things through it.’ What, then, will you call evil? Venomous reptiles and deadly plants, or demons, or any other things capable of troubling human beings? These very things—the ..... subtle things—would not have existed if man had not sinned, on whose account death slipped in. For while man was ......, reptile venom was not active, the effects of evil plants did not operate, harassment by demons did not occur, nor did any other suffering naturally belong to him. But when, because of sin, he fell from being immortal, he became, as I said, susceptible to every kind of suffering.

“But if you say, ‘Why, then, was human nature made susceptible to death at the beginning?’ I tell you: because of free choice. For if we had not been susceptible to death, we could not have been punished for freely chosen sin, since we would have been immortal. And thus, because of our incapacity for suffering, justice too would have been weakened to some further degree, even if we were evil in purpose, since those possessing evil purposes would have been unable to be punished because of their incapacity for suffering.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φύσιν ἔχει ἐμφύειν τὰ κακὰ καὶ τὰ ἀγαθά
lexical_decisions.chosen: does it have a nature capable of producing evil things and good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμφύειν can describe causing things to grow, engendering them, or producing them from within.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it is neither good nor evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: Matter is treated as morally neutral because it lacks conscious choice, not because its products are denied all harmful effects.

lexical_decisions.chosen: skillfully formed shapes
lexical_decisions.rationale: τεχνικός here describes forms displaying craft or art rather than the modern sense “technical.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: his spirit operates it
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐργάζομαι with the accusative presents God’s spirit as the agent working or actuating matter; “works through it” is a possible contextual paraphrase but less formally direct.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐχθρόν τι ἐστιν ἢ ἰσοδύναμον ἢ ἀδύνατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or beyond his power
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀδύνατον literally means “powerless” or “impossible.” In this sequence it is taken as something impossible for God to control, hence “beyond his power”; “anything powerless” is formally possible but contextually less coherent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: venomous reptiles and deadly plants
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰοβόλος means poison- or venom-casting, while θανάσιμος denotes what is deadly or death-dealing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on whose account death slipped in
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine relative οὗ most naturally refers to man. παρεισέρχομαι depicts death as entering alongside or slipping in.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he became susceptible to every kind of suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάθος here includes harmful experiences, afflictions, or suffering, while δεκτικός denotes liability or susceptibility.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of free choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτεξούσιον denotes self-determination or freedom within one’s own authority. “Free will” is possible, but “free choice” maintains the connection with προαίρεσις.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for freely chosen sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective characterizes the transgression as voluntary or self-determined.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ἀπαθὲς πλεῖόν τι ... ἡ καὶ δικαιοσύνη ἐξησθένει
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of our incapacity for suffering, justice too would have been weakened to some further degree
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλεῖόν τι is loosely positioned and may mean “somewhat more” or “in some greater respect.” The rendering preserves its comparative force without specifying an unstated comparison.

source_issues.source_quote: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὢν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;
source_issues.issue: The printed ὢν produces a highly compressed and irregular construction. The translation retains it through “exist as” and treats αὕτη τίκτει as an attendant clause. A commonly plausible conjecture would replace ὢν with the relative ὧν, yielding “is he not himself the cause of the evils that this matter begets?” That conjecture has not been silently inserted into the translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὧν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly five dots between τὰ and λεπτὰ. Its content is unavailable, and no restoration has been supplied; the five-dot gap is retained explicitly in the translation.

The selected edition prints a lacuna of exactly six dots before γὰρ. The missing content is unavailable and has not been restored. English word order places the six-dot gap after “was” so that the surviving genitive absolute can be represented intelligibly without filling the gap.
